standard.title: Significant individuals in empire
standard.description: the role and achievements of a significant individual and/or group connected to the empire and/or expansion
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain the role and achievements of a significant individual in an ancient society (AC9HH7K13) and understand significance as a historical concept (AC9HH8K05). They understand the social and cultural features of the chosen empire (AC9HH8K07) and its turning points (AC9HH8K08). They have not yet applied significance analysis to individuals specifically connected to medieval empire and expansion.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the role and achievements of a significant individual or group connected to the chosen empire or expansion — describing what they did, the conditions that enabled their actions, and the impact and legacy of their achievements on the empire and beyond.

nodes.label: The individual in historical context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the historical context in which the chosen individual operated and explain the conditions that enabled their rise to significance.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of the chosen individual's role with reference to the conditions that enabled it.
nodes.typical_width: The chosen individual situated within the empire's broader context. Examples: Genghis Khan's unification of Mongol tribes enabled by their nomadic military culture; Kublai Khan as first Mongol emperor of China, his administrative approach and relationship to Chinese culture; Selim I capturing Jerusalem or Suleiman the Magnificent expanding to Belgrade; Erik the Red's settlement of Greenland; Columbus, Balboa, Cortés, Montezuma II or Pizarro in the chronology of Spanish conquest.
wider: Compare the leadership styles and successes of Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan — military expansion vs administrative consolidation — to show how different approaches to power can both be significant
Examine the artefacts at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland as possible evidence that the Vikings journeyed to North America 500 years before Columbus, questioning who 'discovered' the Americas

response_modes.reason: Students often attribute empire-building to individual greatness without examining the conditions that made individuals' actions possible. Scaffold the contextualisation: what circumstances enabled this person to act as they did?

success_criteria: Describes the role of the chosen individual in the context of the chosen empire or expansion
Explains at least one condition (social, military, political or cultural) that enabled the individual's rise to significance

nodes.label: Achievements and their significance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the key achievements of the chosen individual and evaluate their significance — describing both what was achieved and why it mattered for the empire and for later history.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two achievements of the chosen individual with an explanation of their significance.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple achievements analysed for immediate and longer-term significance. Examples: Genghis Khan's decimal military organisation, codified laws and policies; Selim I or Suleiman the Magnificent's territorial expansion and governance; Erik the Red's development of Viking settlements in Greenland; key chronological events in the lives of Columbus, Cortés or Pizarro and their significance for the Americas.
wider: Compare historians' interpretations of Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent's achievements to show how the same individual's record can be assessed differently depending on the interpretive lens

Examine Erik the Red's development of Viking settlements in eastern and western Greenland (985 CE) as evidence of expansion beyond the known world — and compare with L'Anse aux Meadows to evaluate the extent of Viking achievement
nodes.hinge_reason: Achievement analysis is the core demand of this descriptor. Students who cannot explain what was achieved and why it mattered — rather than merely narrating events — have not met the standard. Legacy analysis in the next node depends on solid achievement analysis here.

response_modes.reason: Students often narrate a biography rather than analyse achievements. Scaffold the distinction: an achievement is not just something that happened but something that had consequence. Each achievement needs an explicitly reasoned explanation of why it mattered.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two achievements of the chosen individual
Explains why each achievement was significant — not just what happened, but what it changed or enabled

nodes.label: Legacy and historical judgement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the legacy of the chosen individual — explaining what endured from their achievements, how historians have judged their significance, and what their actions mean for our understanding of empire and expansion.
nodes.minimum_width: An explanation of at least one lasting legacy and a reference to how the individual is regarded by historians.
nodes.typical_width: Legacy evaluated across multiple criteria; differing historians' perspectives on the individual's significance; connections between the individual's achievements and ongoing historical developments. Examples: the Mongol legacy in trade connections and cultural exchange; the Viking legacy in settlement and navigation; the contested legacy of Spanish conquest for Indigenous populations and for the modern world.
wider: Examine how historians' interpretations of conquistadores such as Cortés or Pizarro differ — from heroic explorers to colonial oppressors — as a case study in how the same individual can be judged very differently depending on whose perspective is centred
Compare the achievements of Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan across military conquest and cultural administration to evaluate which form of achievement has left a more enduring legacy

response_modes.reason: Legacy assessment integrates contextual understanding (Node 1) and achievement analysis (Node 2). Invest in helping students articulate a coherent historical judgement that draws on both, rather than treating legacy as a separate summary exercise.

success_criteria: Explains at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual and connects it to the empire's or expansion's longer-term history
References at least one historians' judgement and evaluates it against the evidence
